record.original_question: Given an integer N 1, classify all sets A [1; N] such that jAj > N 1=3+", and A occupies at most 2p=3 residue classes modulo p for every prime p < p N. Must any such A essentially be contained in the set of values of a quadratic polynomial? By \essentially" we mean that all, but N o(1) elements of A, lie in such a set. Both the above properties can be weakened, and still the problem would be interesting and di cult; for example, the 2p=3 can be replaced with (1 1)p, and the 1=3 + " can be replaced with N 2 (though this would mean there are more possibilities than just quadratic polynomials to consider). Naively, one may think that such sets A cannot exist, upon applying the following heuristic: if A occupies at most 2=3 of the residue classes mod p for k di erent primes p, then one would expect that A has size at most (2=3)kN, which can be made smaller than 1 by choosing k > c log N, for a certain c > 0. However, this simple heuristic does not give accurate predictions, as it follows by considering the set of all squares in [1; N].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix $\varepsilon > 0$. For an integer $N \geq 1$, consider subsets $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$ satisfying the following two conditions:

(i) $|A| > N^{1/3 + \varepsilon}$;

(ii) for every prime $p < \sqrt{N}$, the set $A$ occupies at most $\lfloor 2p/3 \rfloor$ residue classes modulo $p$ (that is, $|\{a \bmod p : a \in A\}| \leq 2p/3$).

Classify all such sets $A$. In particular, prove or disprove: every such $A$ must be "essentially" contained in the value set $\{f(n) : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ of some quadratic polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, where "essentially" means that all but at most $N^{o(1)}$ elements of $A$ lie in such a value set.

(Variants of interest: replacing the bound $2p/3$ in (ii) by $(1-\delta)p$ for some fixed $\delta \in (0,1)$, and/or replacing the lower bound $N^{1/3+\varepsilon}$ in (i) by $N^\delta$ for some $\delta > 0$, in which case the structured sets to be classified may include more possibilities than just images of quadratic polynomials.)
artifact.category_tag: Inverse sieve problems in additive combinatorics
artifact.status_search_result: The inverse sieve problem in this form (large integer sets occupying few residue classes modulo many primes being essentially algebraic) is a well-known open problem; partial results exist in higher-dimensional analogues (e.g., Helfgott–Venkatesh-style inverse sieve work), but no classification of "square-like" sets in dimension one at the stated density $N^{1/3+\varepsilon}$ is known.

status_evidence.title: The inverse sieve problem in high dimensions
status_evidence.snippet: If a large set of integer points in [0,N]^d occupies few residue classes mod p for many primes p, then it must essentially lie in the solution set of some polynomial equation of low degree.
status_evidence.claim: The inverse sieve problem—classifying integer sets that occupy few residue classes modulo many primes—is an active research area with only partial results known.
